{"self_assessment": "Impact: I proposed the animal, a big side-view fish with the nose on the left, because its outline reads clearly and one run can split round the body. I drew the sketch on the pad and redrew it with the start at the nose so the fall could split into a top line and a belly line, then flatten into the tail stem. I laid the start domino and the whole top line, the longest single stroke in the picture, and closed its tail end. I also laid the links from the start toward the top and belly lines. Late on I re-laid the upper tail fork so the tail finished in time.

Execution: I worked steadily from the first minute to the last. I laid the top line in short, continuous builds, inspected the nose area closely when the fall stalled, and cleared and rebuilt the tangle there. I finished the tail with time to spare and then took my hands off the table so nothing got bumped before the push.

Collaboration: I split the work up front: belly line for Sofia, tail forks for Omar and Hana, top line for me. I kept the table updated on where I was and what I was touching, and I stayed out of Sofia's and Hana's areas while they worked on the nose joins. I credited teammates' good catches openly.

Leadership: I set the direction in the first seconds, assigned roles, and kept the energy up. When the design needed to change, I made the call and got everyone moving on the new plan quickly. In the final minutes I made sure only one person was working on each area, so people weren't undoing each other's work.

I believe my share of the table's result was about 35%.", "my_share_percent": 35}
